sections.title: Pinyin and tones
sections.summary: Mandarin is written in characters, but learners read its sounds through Hanyu Pinyin. This chapter covers the four tones and the neutral tone, the tone changes of 一, 不 and paired third tones, and the initials that trip up English speakers.

rules.title: The four tones and the neutral tone
rules.body: Every Mandarin syllable carries a tone, and the tone changes the word. The first tone is high and level (ā), the second rises like a question (á), the third dips and comes back up (ǎ), the fourth falls sharply (à). A fifth, the neutral tone, is short and light with no mark (ma). The classic set is 妈 mā mother, 麻 má hemp, 马 mǎ horse, 骂 mà to scold, and 吗 ma, the question particle.

rules.title: Where the tone mark goes
rules.body: The mark sits on the main vowel. If the syllable has an a or an e, the mark goes there (hǎo, xiě). Otherwise, if it has ou, the mark goes on the o (gǒu). In every other case it goes on the last vowel letter (duì, liù, jiǔ). The dot of i is replaced by the tone mark: nǐ, jǐ.

examples.en: correct (mark on the last vowel, i)

rules.title: Two third tones in a row
rules.body: When two third-tone syllables meet, the first one is pronounced as a second tone. 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but said ní hǎo; 很好 hěn hǎo sounds like hén hǎo. The spelling does not change, only the pronunciation. Before any other tone, a third tone is usually cut short into a low 'half third' without the final rise (hěn máng, hěn dà).

examples.en: very busy (half third tone, no change)

rules.title: 不 changes before a fourth tone
rules.body: 不 'not' is a fourth-tone word, bù. Before another fourth tone it switches to the second tone, bú, so that two falls do not collide: 不是 bú shì, 不对 bú duì, 不要 bú yào. Before first, second and third tones it stays bù: 不吃 bù chī, 不来 bù lái, 不好 bù hǎo. Many textbooks print the changed tone; many dictionaries do not.

examples.en: is not (changed to bú before 4th tone)

rules.title: 一 changes with the following tone
rules.body: 一 'one' is first tone (yī) on its own, in counting, in numbers like 十一, and in ordinals like 第一. Before a first, second or third tone it becomes fourth tone: 一天 yì tiān, 一年 yì nián, 一起 yì qǐ. Before a fourth tone it becomes second tone: 一个 yí gè, 一样 yí yàng, 一定 yí dìng.

rules.title: The retroflex initials zh, ch, sh, r
rules.body: zh, ch, sh and r are said with the tongue tip curled up and back toward the roof of the mouth. zh is like j in 'judge', ch like ch in 'church', sh like sh in 'shoe', all retroflexed; r is between an English r and the s in 'measure'. Contrast them with the flat z (ts in 'cats'), c (ts with a strong puff of air) and s. After these seven initials the letter i is not 'ee' but a buzzing vowel: zhī, chī, shī, rì, zì, cì, sì.

rules.title: j, q, x and the vowel ü
rules.body: j, q and x are made with the tongue tip down behind the lower teeth, the middle of the tongue high. j is like a light 'j', q like 'ch' with a puff of air, x between s and sh (think 'see' said with a smile). They only occur before i and ü. After j, q, x and y the letter u always means ü (lips rounded while saying 'ee'): 去 qù, 鱼 yú, 句 jù. Only after n and l do the dots stay, to tell 女 nǚ from 努 nǔ and 绿 lǜ from 路 lù.

rules.title: Finals with hidden letters
rules.body: A few finals are written short but said in full. iu stands for iou (六 liù sounds like 'lee-oh'), ui stands for uei (对 duì sounds like 'dway'), and un stands for uen (春 chūn sounds like 'chwun'). When there is no initial, i becomes y and u becomes w: yī, wǔ, yuè. Also watch the e in words like 饿 è and 和 hé, a sound like the u in 'but' or the a in 'about', not the e in 'bed'.

examples.en: five (u written as w with no initial)

rules.title: The neutral tone in everyday words
rules.body: Many second syllables and particles lose their tone and are said short and light: the second half of 妈妈 māma, 爸爸 bàba, 谢谢 xièxie, and the particles 的 de, 了 le, 吗 ma, 呢 ne, plus the plural suffix 们 men. In pinyin a neutral tone simply has no mark. Its actual pitch depends on the tone before it, so just make it short.

exercises.q: How many main tones does Mandarin have, not counting the neutral tone?
exercises.explain: Mandarin has four full tones (high, rising, falling-rising, falling) plus a light neutral tone.

exercises.q: Which syllable carries the sharply falling fourth tone?
exercises.explain: The grave accent à marks the falling fourth tone, as in 骂 mà 'to scold'.

exercises.q: The tone mark in hǎo shows a falling-rising third tone.
exercises.explain: The caron ǎ is the mark of the third tone, which dips and then rises.

exercises.q: 妈 mā is 'mother' and 骂 mà is 'to scold'. Which tone does 马 'horse' have?
exercises.explain: 马 is mǎ, third tone; only the tone separates it from 妈 and 骂.

exercises.q: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but pronounced ___ hǎo (write the first syllable in pinyin with the tone actually used)
exercises.explain: When two third tones meet, the first is said as a second tone: ní hǎo.

exercises.q: In 不是 'is not', 不 is pronounced
exercises.explain: Before a fourth tone (shì), 不 changes from bù to the rising bú.

exercises.q: In 不好 'not good', 不 is pronounced
exercises.explain: 好 hǎo is third tone, so 不 keeps its normal fourth tone bù.

exercises.q: 一 is pronounced yí before a fourth-tone syllable, as in 一个 yí gè.
exercises.explain: Before a fourth tone, 一 switches to the second tone yí.

exercises.q: 一天 'one day': 一 is pronounced ___ tiān (pinyin with tone mark)
exercises.explain: Before a first, second or third tone, 一 becomes fourth tone yì.

exercises.q: 一样 'the same': 一 is pronounced
exercises.explain: 样 yàng is fourth tone, so 一 becomes the rising yí.

exercises.q: Which initial is retroflex, with the tongue tip curled back?
exercises.explain: zh, ch, sh and r are the retroflex initials; z, c, s are flat and j, q, x are palatal.

exercises.q: Pinyin q is pronounced like the k in English 'kite'.
exercises.explain: q is close to the ch in 'cheap' with a strong puff of air, never like k.

exercises.q: In 去 qù, the letter u actually represents
exercises.explain: After j, q, x and y the letter u always stands for ü.

exercises.q: 女 'woman' keeps the dots on its u in pinyin: ___ (write the pinyin with tone mark)
exercises.explain: After n and l the dots are kept to distinguish nǚ from nǔ.

exercises.q: Which pair of syllables differs only in tone?
exercises.explain: mā and mà share the same sounds and differ only in tone (first vs fourth).

exercises.q: In 妈妈 māma the second syllable has the neutral tone and is said short and light.
exercises.explain: Reduplicated family words lose the tone on the second syllable.

exercises.answer: 你 好 吗？
我 不 是 老师。
他 很 好。

exercises.q: When two third tones meet, as in 很好 hěn hǎo, the first one is pronounced as
exercises.explain: The first of two third tones becomes a second tone: hén hǎo.

exercises.q: Where does the tone mark go in the syllable xie (写 'to write')?
exercises.explain: If a syllable contains a or e, the mark goes on that vowel: xiě.

exercises.q: 不对 'wrong': 不 is pronounced ___ (pinyin with tone mark)
exercises.explain: 对 duì is fourth tone, so 不 shifts to the second tone bú.

pairs: retroflex, like j in 'judge' with the tongue curled back
like ts in 'cats' with a puff of air
between s and sh, tongue tip down, only before i and ü
retroflex, between English r and the s in 'measure'

exercises.q: When a syllable has no initial, the final i is written y (yī), and u is written w (wǔ).
exercises.explain: Pinyin spells 一 as yī and 五 as wǔ because they have no initial consonant.

exercises.q: The letter i in zhi, chi, shi, ri, zi, ci, si is
exercises.explain: After these seven initials, i is a buzzing sound made with the tongue in the same place as the consonant.

exercises.answer: 我 也 很 好。

sections.title: Characters: strokes, radicals and components
sections.summary: Chinese characters are built from a small set of strokes and reusable components. Knowing stroke order, radicals and phonetic parts makes characters easier to write, look up and remember, and explains the split between simplified and traditional forms.

rules.title: The basic strokes
rules.body: Characters are written with a handful of strokes: 横 héng (horizontal, left to right), 竖 shù (vertical, top to bottom), 撇 piě (falling to the left), 捺 nà (falling to the right), 点 diǎn (dot), 提 tí (rising flick), 钩 gōu (hook) and 折 zhé (a turn within one stroke). 永 yǒng 'forever' is famous for containing all the main stroke types in eight strokes.

examples.en: one: a single horizontal stroke 横
ten: a horizontal then a vertical
person: a left-falling 撇 and a right-falling 捺
forever: shows all the basic strokes

rules.title: Stroke order basics
rules.body: Write from top to bottom and from left to right. A horizontal stroke comes before a vertical that crosses it (十: 一 then 丨). Left-falling 撇 comes before right-falling 捺 (人). Outer parts come before inner parts (同), but a box is closed last: in 国 you write the frame, then 玉, then the bottom line. A central stroke comes before symmetrical sides (小). Correct order makes handwriting fluent and lets stroke-based dictionaries and input methods find the character.

examples.en: country: frame, inside, then close the box
small: middle stroke first, then the sides

rules.title: Radicals carry a hint of meaning
rules.body: Most characters contain a radical (部首 bùshǒu), a component used to classify them in dictionaries and often hinting at the meaning. 氵 (water) appears in 河 river, 海 sea and 湖 lake; 讠 (speech) in 说 speak, 话 words and 语 language; 口 (mouth) in 吃 eat, 喝 drink and 叫 call; 女 (woman) in 妈 mother, 姐 older sister and 她 she. There are 214 traditional Kangxi radicals, but a few dozen cover most everyday characters.

rules.title: Radicals change shape on the side
rules.body: Several radicals have a squeezed form when they sit on the left of a character. 人 person becomes 亻 (你, 他, 们), 水 water becomes 氵 (河, 汉), 手 hand becomes 扌 (打, 找), 心 heart becomes 忄 (忙, 快), 言 speech becomes 讠 (说, 请), 金 metal becomes 钅 (钱, 银), 食 food becomes 饣 (饭, 饿) and 丝 silk becomes 纟 (红, 给). Learning these pairs lets you spot the meaning hint quickly.

examples.en: cooked rice, meal (饣 from 食)

rules.title: Phonetic components hint at the sound
rules.body: About four fifths of characters are 形声字 xíngshēngzì: one part suggests the meaning, the other the sound. 马 mǎ gives its sound to 妈 mā, 吗 ma and 码 mǎ, while 女, 口 and 石 add the meaning. 青 qīng gives 清 qīng clear, 请 qǐng please, 情 qíng feeling and 晴 qíng sunny. The tone and sometimes the initial can differ, so the hint is approximate, but it is a powerful memory aid.

examples.en: mother: 女 for meaning, 马 for sound
please: 讠 for meaning, 青 for sound
clear: 氵 for meaning, 青 for sound
question particle: 口 for meaning, 马 for sound

rules.title: Pictographs and compound ideographs
rules.body: A minority of characters are simplified pictures: 日 sun, 月 moon, 山 mountain, 人 person, 木 tree, 口 mouth. Some are abstract signs: 一 二 三 one two three, 上 up, 下 down. Others combine meanings: 休 rest is a person 亻 leaning on a tree 木; 明 bright is sun 日 plus moon 月; 好 good is woman 女 plus child 子; 林 forest is two trees. These stories are useful for memory even where the real etymology is more complicated.

examples.en: to rest: 亻 person + 木 tree
bright: 日 sun + 月 moon

rules.title: Simplified and traditional characters
rules.body: Mainland China reformed the script in the 1950s and 1960s, cutting strokes from about two thousand common characters. Simplified characters are standard in mainland China, Singapore and Malaysia; traditional characters remain standard in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau. Many characters are the same in both (我, 你, 好, 人), and the differences follow patterns: 讠/言, 门/門, 车/車, 马/馬, 学/學, 国/國. This app uses simplified characters.

rules.title: Characters, syllables and words
rules.body: Each character is one syllable, and the script has no spaces. A word may be one character (人 person, 好 good) but most modern words have two (学生 xuéshēng student, 老师 lǎoshī teacher, 中国 Zhōngguó China). A character is a 字 zì; a word is a 词 cí. Reading means recognising which characters group into words. Count strokes with 笔画 bǐhuà: 口 has three strokes, 你 has seven.

exercises.q: Which stroke is 横 héng?
exercises.explain: 横 héng is the horizontal stroke, written from left to right.

exercises.q: The general direction of stroke order is
options: bottom to top, right to left
top to bottom, left to right
exercises.explain: Characters are written from top to bottom and from left to right.

exercises.q: In 十 'ten', the horizontal stroke is written before the vertical one.
exercises.explain: A horizontal stroke comes before a vertical stroke that crosses it.

exercises.q: In 国 'country', which stroke is written last?
options: the left side of the box
the bottom line that closes the box
the top line of the box
exercises.explain: An enclosure is closed last: frame, then the inside, then the bottom line.

exercises.q: The radical shared by 妈, 姐 and 她 is ___ (character or pinyin)
exercises.explain: 女 'woman' is the radical of many characters for female people.

exercises.q: 河 'river', 海 'sea' and 湖 'lake' share the radical
exercises.explain: The three-dot water radical 氵 marks characters connected with water.

exercises.q: In 妈 mā 'mother', the component 马 mǎ is
exercises.explain: 女 gives the meaning 'woman', 马 gives the sound ma.

exercises.q: Most Chinese characters are pure pictures of what they mean.
exercises.explain: About 80% are meaning-plus-sound compounds; true pictographs are a small minority.

exercises.q: 休 'rest' combines 亻 person and 木 tree, a person leaning on a tree. This type of character is a
exercises.explain: A compound ideograph joins two meanings to make a new one.

exercises.q: The simplified form of traditional 國 'country' is ___
exercises.explain: 國 was simplified to 国, with 玉 inside the box.

exercises.q: Where are traditional characters the standard script?
exercises.explain: Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau keep traditional characters; the others use simplified.

exercises.q: Simplified characters were introduced in mainland China in the 1950s and 1960s.
exercises.explain: The script reform of 1956 and 1964 produced today's simplified set.

exercises.q: How many strokes does 口 'mouth' have?
exercises.explain: 口 is written in three strokes: the left side, the top-and-right in one turning stroke, and the bottom.

exercises.q: Each Chinese character stands for
exercises.explain: A character is always exactly one spoken syllable.

exercises.q: Most modern Mandarin words consist of two characters, such as 学生 xuéshēng 'student'.
exercises.explain: Two-character words are the norm in modern Chinese, though many basic words are single characters.

exercises.q: The person radical in its left-side form, as in 你 and 他, is written ___
exercises.explain: 人 is squeezed into 亻 (called 单人旁) when it stands on the left.

exercises.answer: 这 是 什么 字？
我 会 写 汉字。
这个 字 有 几 笔？
exercises.en: How many strokes does this character have?

exercises.q: In 吃 'eat', 喝 'drink' and 叫 'call', the 口 radical signals
options: a meaning connected with the mouth
exercises.explain: 口 'mouth' is the meaning radical for eating, drinking and speaking.

exercises.q: In 小 'small' the middle vertical stroke is written first, then the two sides.
exercises.explain: A central stroke is written before symmetrical left and right parts.

exercises.q: The dictionary radical of 想 xiǎng 'to think' is
exercises.explain: 想 has 心 'heart' at the bottom as its radical; 相 is the phonetic.

exercises.q: Which pair shows simplified → traditional?
exercises.explain: 说 is the simplified form and 說 the traditional, with 讠 and 言 as the speech radical.

exercises.q: The phonetic component shared by 吗, 妈 and 码 is ___
exercises.explain: 马 mǎ lends its sound to all three characters.

exercises.answer: 汉字 很 有意思。

exercises.q: When a character has a left part and a right part, the right part is written first.
exercises.explain: Left comes before right: in 你 the 亻 is written before the right side.

sections.title: Basic sentence patterns with 是, 有, 在
sections.summary: Mandarin sentences follow subject-verb-object and verbs never change form. This chapter builds the first patterns with 是 'to be', 有 'to have / there is' and 在 'to be at', and shows how to negate each one correctly.

rules.title: Subject, verb, object: no endings
rules.body: The basic order is subject, verb, object, as in English: 我爱你 'I love you', 我学中文 'I study Chinese'. Verbs never change for person, number or tense: 是 is 'am', 'is' and 'are'; 学 is 'study', 'studies' and 'studied'. The subject is often dropped when it is clear from context.

rules.title: Pronouns
rules.body: 我 wǒ I, 你 nǐ you, 他 tā he, 她 tā she, 它 tā it; add 们 men for plurals: 我们 we, 你们 you (plural), 他们 they. 他, 她 and 它 sound identical and differ only in writing. 您 nín is the polite 'you' for elders, customers and strangers. Pronouns do not change for subject or object: 我爱你, 你爱我.

rules.title: 是 links two nouns
rules.body: 是 shì 'to be' connects a subject with a noun: 我是学生 'I am a student', 他是老师 'he is a teacher', 这是我的书 'this is my book'. Do not use 是 before a plain adjective; Chinese says 她很高 'she is tall' with 很, not 她是高. 是 is usually unstressed in speech.

examples.en: She is tall. (no 是 before an adjective)

rules.title: Negating 是 with 不
rules.body: Put 不 bù directly before 是: 他不是老师 'he is not a teacher', 这不是我的 'this is not mine'. 不 is pronounced bú here because 是 is fourth tone. To answer a yes/no question you repeat the verb: 是 'yes (it is)', 不是 'no (it is not)'.

examples.roman: Zhè bú shì wǒ de shū.
Bú shì, wǒ shì Měiguó rén.

rules.title: 有 means 'to have', and its negative is 没有
rules.body: 有 yǒu expresses possession: 我有一个哥哥 'I have an older brother', 她有车 'she has a car'. 有 is the one verb that is never negated with 不; it takes 没 méi instead: 我没有钱 'I have no money'. In the negative the 有 can be dropped in short answers: 没有 or just 没.

rules.title: 有 for 'there is / there are'
rules.body: Place + 有 + thing says what exists somewhere: 桌子上有一本书 'there is a book on the table', 附近有银行 'there is a bank nearby', 这儿没有人 'there is nobody here'. The place comes first; words like 上 'on', 里 'in' follow the noun: 桌子上, 家里.

examples.roman: Zhuōzi shang yǒu yì běn shū.
examples.en: There is a book on the table.

rules.title: 在 as the verb 'to be at'
rules.body: 在 zài places a person or thing somewhere: 我在家 'I am at home', 他在北京 'he is in Beijing', 书在桌子上 'the book is on the table'. Negate with 不在: 他不在 'he is not here / not in'. 在哪儿 asks 'where': 你在哪儿？

rules.title: 在 + place before an action verb
rules.body: To say where an action happens, 在 + place goes before the verb, not after it as in English: 我在家吃饭 'I eat at home', 她在北京工作 'she works in Beijing', 他们在图书馆学习 'they study in the library'. Keep the order subject + 在 place + verb + object.

rules.title: 也 and 都 go before the verb
rules.body: Adverbs such as 也 yě 'also' and 都 dōu 'all, both' sit between the subject and the verb, never at the end: 我也是学生 'I am also a student', 我们都在家 'we are all at home'. When both appear, 也 comes before 都: 他们也都是老师. With a negative, 都不 means 'none': 我们都不是老师.

examples.en: None of them is a teacher.

rules.title: 这 and 那 with 是
rules.body: 这 zhè 'this' and 那 nà 'that' are the usual subjects of 是 sentences: 这是什么？ 'what is this?', 那是我的车 'that is my car'. For places use 这儿 zhèr 'here' and 那儿 nàr 'there' (or 这里, 那里): 他在那儿 'he is there'.

exercises.q: Choose the correct sentence for 'I am a student.'
exercises.explain: Subject + 是 + noun: 我是学生.

exercises.q: 我___学生。(am)
exercises.explain: 是 links the subject with a noun and never changes form.

exercises.q: 'He is not a teacher.'
exercises.explain: 是 is negated with 不 placed directly before it.

exercises.q: To say 'I don't have money' you say 我不有钱.
exercises.explain: 有 is negated with 没, never 不: 我没有钱.

exercises.q: 我___有时间。(do not have)
exercises.explain: 没 is the only negator used with 有.

exercises.q: 'She is in Beijing.'
exercises.explain: 在 is the verb for being located somewhere.

exercises.answer: 我 是 学生。
他 不 是 老师。
我 有 一个 哥哥。

exercises.q: 'There is a book on the table.' 桌子上___一本书。
exercises.explain: Place + 有 + thing expresses existence.

exercises.q: 是 is normally not used before a plain adjective: 她很高, not 她是高.
exercises.explain: Adjectives work as predicates on their own, usually with 很.

exercises.q: 'I eat at home.'
exercises.explain: 在 + place comes before the verb, not after it.

exercises.q: 他___家吗？(is he at home?)
exercises.explain: 在 + place says where someone is.

exercises.q: 'We are all students.'
exercises.explain: 都 goes between the subject and the verb.

exercises.q: 也 'also' goes before the verb: 我也是学生.
exercises.explain: Adverbs like 也 and 都 always precede the verb.

exercises.answer: 她 在 北京 工作。

exercises.q: The polite form of 'you' is
exercises.explain: 您 nín is used for elders, customers and people you want to show respect to.

exercises.q: 这儿___人。(there is nobody here)
exercises.explain: Existence with 有 is negated as 没有.

exercises.q: 'That is not my book.'
exercises.explain: 不 goes right before 是: 那不是...

exercises.q: Chinese verbs change form for person and number, like English am / is / are.
exercises.explain: 是 is the same for every subject; verbs have no endings.

exercises.q: 我有两个姐姐。 means
exercises.explain: 有 is 'to have' and 姐姐 is 'older sister'.

exercises.answer: 我们 都 不 在 家。
exercises.en: None of us is at home.

exercises.q: 'He is not at school.'
exercises.explain: 不 precedes 在, and 在 precedes the place.

exercises.q: 她___我的老师。(is)
exercises.explain: 是 connects 她 with the noun 老师.

exercises.q: 没 negates 有, while 不 negates 是 and 在.
exercises.explain: 没有 'not have', 不是 'is not', 不在 'is not at'.

exercises.q: 'Is there a bank nearby?' 附近___银行吗？
exercises.explain: 有 after a place means 'there is'.

sections.title: Measure words and numbers
sections.summary: Chinese counts with a simple decimal system, but every number must be joined to its noun by a measure word. This chapter covers the numbers, the all-purpose 个 and the common measure words, the 两 versus 二 rule and ordinals with 第.

rules.title: Numbers 0 to 99
rules.body: 零 líng 0, 一 yī 1, 二 èr 2, 三 sān 3, 四 sì 4, 五 wǔ 5, 六 liù 6, 七 qī 7, 八 bā 8, 九 jiǔ 9, 十 shí 10. Teens are 十 + digit: 十一 11, 十二 12. Tens are digit + 十: 二十 20, 三十 30; then add the unit: 二十一 21, 九十九 99. No irregular forms at all.

rules.title: Hundreds, thousands and 万
rules.body: 百 bǎi hundred, 千 qiān thousand, 万 wàn ten thousand. Chinese groups by four digits, so 100,000 is 十万 'ten ten-thousands' and 1,000,000 is 一百万. A zero inside a number is read as 零: 一百零五 105. When a number ends in tens or hundreds, the final unit can be dropped: 一百一 110, but spelling it out as 一百一十 is always safe. 一百 is said yì bǎi and 一千 yì qiān.

rules.title: Number + measure word + noun
rules.body: You cannot put a number directly on a noun. A measure word (量词 liàngcí) must stand between them, a bit like 'two cups of tea' or 'three sheets of paper', except that every noun needs one: 一个人 'one person', 三本书 'three books', 两杯茶 'two cups of tea'. 三书 is wrong.

rules.title: 个, the all-purpose measure word
rules.body: 个 gè (usually neutral tone, ge) is the default measure word for people and for anything without a specific one: 一个人, 两个苹果 'two apples', 三个问题 'three questions', 一个星期 'one week'. If you forget the correct measure word, 个 will be understood, though 位 wèi is the polite choice for people: 两位老师.

rules.title: Common specific measure words
rules.body: 本 běn bound things (书 book, 杂志 magazine); 杯 bēi cups of (茶, 咖啡); 只 zhī animals (猫 cat, 狗 dog) and one of a pair; 条 tiáo long flexible things (鱼 fish, 路 road, 裤子 trousers); 张 zhāng flat things (纸 paper, 桌子 table, 票 ticket); 件 jiàn clothes and matters (衣服, 事); 辆 liàng vehicles (车); 口 kǒu family members; 块 kuài pieces and money; 瓶 píng bottles; 家 jiā shops and companies; 把 bǎ things with a handle (椅子 chair, 伞 umbrella); 支 zhī pens.

rules.title: 这, 那, 哪 and 几 take measure words too
rules.body: Demonstratives and question words behave like numbers: 这个人 'this person', 那本书 'that book', 哪个 'which one', 几本书 'how many books'. A number can be added: 这两本书 'these two books'. 这些 zhèxiē and 那些 nàxiē mean 'these' and 'those' without another measure word.

rules.title: 两 versus 二
rules.body: Before a measure word, 'two' is 两 liǎng, not 二: 两个人, 两本书, 两杯咖啡. 二 èr is used in counting (一, 二, 三), inside compound numbers (十二 12, 二十 20, 二十二 22), in ordinals (第二) and when reading digits aloud. Before 百, 千 and 万, 两 is the usual choice (两百, 两千, 两万), though 二百 is also heard. 两 never appears in 十二 or 二十.

rules.title: Ordinals with 第
rules.body: Put 第 dì before a number to make an ordinal: 第一 first, 第二 second (never 第两), 第三 third, 第十 tenth. A measure word and noun can follow: 第一个 'the first one', 第三课 'lesson three', 第二天 'the next day'. Months and some dates count without 第: 一月 January, 一号 the 1st.

rules.title: Money and halves
rules.body: Prices use 块 kuài (written 元 yuán) for the main unit and 毛 máo (written 角 jiǎo) for tenths: 三块五 'three kuai fifty', 十块钱 'ten kuai'. 多少钱 asks 'how much'. 半 bàn 'half' goes before the measure word on its own (半个小时 'half an hour') and after it for 'and a half' (一个半小时 'an hour and a half').

exercises.q: 'three books'
exercises.explain: A measure word must stand between number and noun; 本 is the one for books.

exercises.q: 一___人 (one person; the all-purpose measure word)
exercises.explain: 个 is the default measure word, used for people.

exercises.q: 'two people'
exercises.explain: Before a measure word, two is 两, not 二.

exercises.q: 二 is used directly before a measure word: 二个人.
exercises.explain: Before a measure word you must use 两: 两个人.

exercises.q: 'twenty-two'
exercises.explain: Inside compound numbers, two is always 二: 二十二.

exercises.q: 我有___个姐姐。(two)
exercises.explain: 两 is used for 'two' before measure words.

exercises.q: 'the third' is
exercises.explain: 第 before a number makes an ordinal: 第三.

exercises.q: 'Second' is 第二, not 第两.
exercises.explain: Ordinals always use 二: 第二.

exercises.answer: 我 有 三 本 书。
他 家 有 四 口 人。
exercises.en: There are four people in his family.

exercises.q: 105 is
exercises.explain: A zero inside a number is read 零: 一百零五.

exercises.q: 一万 means
exercises.explain: 万 is ten thousand; Chinese groups numbers by four digits.

exercises.q: 这件衣服三十___钱。(spoken unit of money)
exercises.explain: 块 is the everyday word for the yuan; 元 is the written form.

exercises.q: Which measure word goes with a dog? 一___狗
exercises.explain: 只 is the measure word for most animals.

exercises.q: 一百一十 means
exercises.explain: 一百 100 plus 一十 10 gives 110; 101 would be 一百零一.

exercises.q: Because 10,000 has its own word 万, 100,000 is 十万.
exercises.explain: Chinese counts in units of 万, so 100,000 is 'ten 万'.

exercises.q: 我要一___咖啡。(a cup of)
exercises.explain: 杯 is the measure word for cups and glasses of a drink.

exercises.q: 'this book'
exercises.explain: 这 takes a measure word like a number: 这本书; 这些书 means 'these books'.

exercises.answer: 这 是 第一 课。

exercises.q: 'twelve' is
exercises.explain: Compound numbers use 二: 十二; 二十 is twenty.

exercises.q: 两 replaces 二 inside compound numbers, so twelve is 十两.
exercises.explain: 两 is only for counting things before a measure word; twelve is 十二.

exercises.q: ___一 (first)
exercises.explain: 第 turns a number into an ordinal.

exercises.q: Which measure word is used specifically for counting members of a family? 你家有几___人？
exercises.explain: 口 'mouth' counts the people in a household.

exercises.answer: 我 要 两 杯 茶。
exercises.en: I want two cups of tea.

exercises.q: 'an hour and a half'
exercises.explain: 半 goes after the measure word for 'and a half': 一个半小时.

exercises.q: 一百 is pronounced yì bǎi, with 一 taking the fourth tone before the third-tone 百.
exercises.explain: 一 becomes yì before first, second and third tones.

sections.title: Questions
sections.summary: Chinese questions keep the word order of statements. This chapter covers the particles 吗 and 呢, question words that stay in place, the A-not-A pattern, choice questions with 还是, and how to ask 'how many' with 几 or 多少.

rules.title: Yes/no questions with 吗
rules.body: Add 吗 ma to the end of a statement and it becomes a yes/no question; nothing else moves: 你是学生吗？ 'Are you a student?', 他在家吗？ 'Is he at home?'. Answer by repeating the verb, with 不 or 没 for 'no': 是 / 不是, 在 / 不在, 有 / 没有.

examples.roman: Tā zài jiā ma? Bú zài.

examples.en: Do you have an older brother? Yes.

rules.title: 呢 for 'and ...?' and 'where is ...?'
rules.body: 呢 ne after a noun or pronoun bounces a question back: 我很好，你呢？ 'I'm fine, and you?'. After a noun on its own it asks where something is: 我的书呢？ 'Where's my book?'. 呢 is also used at the end of question-word questions to soften them: 你去哪儿呢？

examples.en: So what would you like to eat?

rules.title: Question words stay in place
rules.body: 什么 shénme what, 谁 shéi who, 哪儿 nǎr where, 哪 nǎ which (+ measure word), 什么时候 shénme shíhou when, 为什么 wèishénme why, 怎么 zěnme how, 怎么样 zěnmeyàng how is it. The question word sits where the answer would be: 他是谁？ 'Who is he?' (answer 他是我哥哥), 你叫什么名字？ 'What is your name?'. Do not add 吗.

rules.title: A-not-A questions
rules.body: Instead of 吗 you can repeat the verb or adjective with 不 in between: 你是不是学生？ 'Are you a student (or not)?', 你去不去？ 'Are you going?', 好不好？ 'Is it OK?'. With 有 the negative is 没: 你有没有时间？ A-not-A is neutral in tone and never combines with 吗.

rules.title: 几 and 多少 for 'how many'
rules.body: 几 jǐ expects a small number, usually under ten, and must be followed by a measure word: 几个人 'how many people', 你几岁？ 'how old are you?' (to a child), 几点？ 'what time?'. 多少 duōshao works for any amount and the measure word is optional: 多少钱 'how much money', 多少人 'how many people', 你的电话号码是多少？ 'what is your phone number?'.

examples.roman: Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?
examples.en: How many people are in your family?
How many students does your school have?

rules.title: 多 + adjective: how old, how tall, how far
rules.body: 多 duō before an adjective asks about degree: 多大 how old / how big, 多高 how tall, 多长 how long, 多远 how far, 多长时间 how long (time). 你多大？ is the normal 'how old are you?' for teenagers and adults; 您多大年纪？ is polite for older people.

examples.en: How far is it from here?

rules.title: 还是 in choice questions, 或者 in statements
rules.body: 'Or' in a question is 还是 háishi: 你喝茶还是咖啡？ 'Do you drink tea or coffee?', 他是老师还是学生？ No 吗 is added. In statements 'or' is 或者 huòzhě: 我喝茶或者咖啡都行 'tea or coffee, either is fine'.

examples.en: Do you drink tea or coffee?

examples.roman: Nǐ jīntiān qù háishi míngtiān qù?
examples.en: Are you going today or tomorrow?
Tea or coffee, either is fine.

rules.title: Tag questions: 好吗, 对吗, 是不是
rules.body: A short tag turns a statement into a request for agreement: 我们去吃饭，好吗？ 'Let's go eat, OK?', 你是北京人，对吗？ 'You're from Beijing, right?', 他很忙，是不是？ 'He's busy, isn't he?'. 行吗 xíng ma and 可以吗 kěyǐ ma ask whether something is acceptable.

examples.roman: Wǒmen qù chī fàn, hǎo ma?
Nǐ shì Běijīng rén, duì ma?
Tā hěn máng, shì bu shì?

rules.title: Answering yes and no
rules.body: There is no single word for 'yes' and 'no'. Repeat the verb for yes and negate it for no: 你是学生吗？ 是。/ 不是。; 你有钱吗？ 有。/ 没有。; 你去吗？ 去。/ 不去。 对 duì 'right' and 不对 'wrong' answer statements, and 好 hǎo accepts a suggestion.

examples.en: Do you have a car? No.

examples.roman: Tā shì Zhōngguó rén ba? Duì.

exercises.q: Turn 你是学生。 into a yes/no question.
exercises.explain: 吗 goes at the very end; nothing else moves.

exercises.q: 你好___？(question particle)
exercises.explain: 吗 at the end makes a yes/no question: 'How are you?'

exercises.q: 我很好，你___？ (and you?)
exercises.explain: 呢 after a pronoun means 'and what about ...?'

exercises.q: Question words stay in the position of the answer: 你叫什么名字？
exercises.explain: 什么 sits where the name would go; nothing moves to the front.

exercises.q: 'Who is he?'
exercises.explain: 谁 takes the place of the answer after 是.

exercises.answer: 你 是 老师 吗？
他 是 谁？

exercises.q: The A-not-A form of 你有时间吗？ is
exercises.explain: 有 is repeated with 没 in between: 有没有.

exercises.q: You can combine A-not-A with 吗: 你是不是学生吗？
exercises.explain: A-not-A is already a question; adding 吗 is ungrammatical.

exercises.q: 你是___是中国人？(A-not-A)
exercises.explain: The verb is repeated with 不 between: 是不是.

exercises.q: 'How old are you?' (asking a small child)
exercises.explain: 几 is used for small expected numbers; 岁 acts as its own measure word.

exercises.q: 'How much is it?'
exercises.explain: 多少 asks about any amount and takes 钱 directly.

exercises.q: 几 is used when a small number is expected and must be followed by a measure word: 几个人.
exercises.explain: 几 behaves like a number and needs a measure word.

exercises.q: 现在___点？(what time is it?)
exercises.explain: 几点 asks the hour; 点 serves as the measure word.

exercises.answer: 你 喝 茶 还是 咖啡？
exercises.en: Do you drink tea or coffee?

exercises.q: 你是学生___老师？ (or, in a question)
exercises.explain: 还是 is 'or' in questions; 或者 is for statements.

exercises.q: 或者 is used for 'or' in statements and 还是 in questions.
exercises.explain: 你喝茶还是咖啡？ but 茶或者咖啡都行.

exercises.q: Answer 'yes' to 你有哥哥吗？
exercises.explain: Repeat the verb of the question: 有.

exercises.q: 我的书___？(where is my book? – particle)
exercises.explain: 呢 after a noun on its own asks where it is.

exercises.q: 'How do you say this in Chinese?' 这个用中文___说？
exercises.explain: 怎么 'how' goes before the verb 说.

exercises.answer: 你 有 没有 中国 朋友？

exercises.q: 'How tall are you?'
exercises.explain: 多 + adjective asks about degree: 多高.

exercises.q: 多少 can be used with or without a measure word: 多少人 and 多少个人 are both fine.
exercises.explain: Unlike 几, 多少 does not require a measure word.

exercises.q: 'Which one?'
exercises.explain: 哪 + measure word means 'which'; 哪儿 means 'where'.

exercises.q: 我们去吃饭，好___？(tag question)
exercises.explain: 好吗 asks 'OK?' after a suggestion.

exercises.answer: 你 什么时候 来？

exercises.q: 你是___国人？ (which)
exercises.explain: 哪 + measure word or noun means 'which'; 哪国 is 'which country'.

sections.title: Aspect: 了, 过, 在/正在, 着
sections.summary: Chinese verbs have no tenses; instead, particles show whether an action is completed, experienced, in progress or a continuing state. This chapter explains 了, 过, 在/正在 and 着, and the mistakes English speakers typically make with them.

rules.title: No tense: time words do the work
rules.body: The verb never changes for past, present or future. 我去北京 can be 'I go', 'I went' or 'I will go'; the time word settles it: 我昨天去北京 'I went to Beijing yesterday', 我明天去北京 'I'm going tomorrow'. The particles in this chapter add aspect, that is, how the action unfolds, not when it happens.

rules.title: 了 after the verb: a completed action
rules.body: 了 le directly after a verb marks the action as completed, usually with an object that has a number or is specific: 我吃了三个苹果 'I ate three apples', 他买了一本书 'he bought a book', 我昨天看了一个电影. With a bare object, verb + 了 + object sounds unfinished (我吃了饭...), so either add detail or move 了 to the end: 我吃饭了.

examples.roman: Wǒ chī le sān ge píngguǒ.
Tā mǎi le yì běn shū.

rules.title: Negating a completed action with 没
rules.body: A completed action is negated with 没 méi (or 没有) and the 了 disappears: 我没吃饭 'I didn't eat', 他没来 'he didn't come', 我没买书. Never combine 没 with 了. 不 negates habits, intentions and the future: 我不吃早饭 'I don't eat breakfast'.

rules.title: 了 at the end of the sentence: a new situation
rules.body: Sentence-final 了 signals that things have changed or a new state has begun: 下雨了 'it's raining (now)', 我饿了 'I'm hungry (now)', 他二十岁了 'he is twenty now', 我不去了 'I'm not going after all'. It can also simply signal that an event has happened: 他来了 'he has come'. This 了 says nothing about the past by itself.

rules.title: Pitfalls with 了
rules.body: Do not use 了 for every past event. Habitual actions take no 了: 我以前每天跑步 'I used to run every day'. 是 and other state verbs do not take verb-了: 他以前是老师, not 他是了老师. Duration sentences put 了 after the verb: 我学了两年中文 'I studied Chinese for two years'; adding a second 了 at the end means the study continues: 我学了两年中文了 'I have been studying for two years (so far)'.

examples.en: I used to run every day. (no 了)
He was a teacher before. (no 了 after 是)

examples.roman: Wǒ xué le liǎng nián Zhōngwén.
examples.en: I studied Chinese for two years.

examples.roman: Wǒ xué le liǎng nián Zhōngwén le.
examples.en: I have been studying Chinese for two years.

rules.title: 过: experience, 'ever / before'
rules.body: 过 guo after a verb says that something has happened at least once in the past, as an experience: 我去过中国 'I have been to China', 你吃过北京烤鸭吗？ 'have you ever eaten Peking duck?'. The negative is 没...过: 我没去过日本, often strengthened with 从来 'never': 我从来没吃过. Compare 他去了北京 'he went to Beijing (and may still be there)' with 他去过北京 'he has been to Beijing'.

examples.roman: Nǐ chī guo Běijīng kǎoyā ma?
examples.en: Have you ever eaten Peking duck?

examples.roman: Wǒ cónglái méi qù guo Rìběn.
examples.en: I have never been to Japan.

rules.title: 在 / 正在: an action in progress
rules.body: 在 zài before the verb means the action is going on: 我在吃饭 'I'm eating', 他在看书 'he is reading'. 正在 zhèngzài stresses 'right now, in the middle of': 我们正在上课. A final 呢 ne is often added: 他在睡觉呢 'he's sleeping'. The negative is 没(有)在: 他没在看书 'he isn't reading'.

examples.en: We are in class right now.

rules.title: 着: a continuing state
rules.body: 着 zhe after a verb describes a state that continues after the action: 门开着 'the door is open', 他坐着 'he is sitting', 她穿着红衣服 'she is wearing red'. Place + verb + 着 describes where something is: 墙上挂着一张画 'a picture hangs on the wall'. Verb-着 can also describe the manner of a second verb: 他笑着说 'he said with a smile', 我们坐着聊 'let's chat sitting down'.

examples.roman: Qiáng shang guà zhe yì zhāng huà.
examples.en: A picture is hanging on the wall.

rules.title: 要...了 and 快...了: about to happen
rules.body: An imminent event is framed with 要 or 快 before the verb and 了 at the end: 我要走了 'I'm leaving now', 快下雨了 'it's about to rain', 火车快到了 'the train is almost here', 他快三十岁了 'he's nearly thirty'. 就要...了 is used when the time is specified: 明天就要考试了.

exercises.q: 'I ate three apples.'
exercises.explain: 了 after the verb marks the completed action with a counted object.

exercises.q: 我昨天买___一本书。(completed action)
exercises.explain: Verb + 了 + counted object: 买了一本书.

exercises.q: Negate 我吃了饭。 ('I didn't eat')
exercises.explain: Completed actions are negated with 没 and the 了 is dropped.

exercises.q: 了 is a past-tense marker that must be used with every past action.
exercises.explain: 了 marks completion or change, not tense; habitual past actions take no 了.

exercises.q: 下雨了 means
exercises.explain: Sentence-final 了 marks a new situation: it is raining now.

exercises.q: 你去___中国吗？(ever been)
exercises.explain: 过 after the verb asks about past experience.

exercises.q: 'He has been to Beijing (at some point).'
exercises.explain: 过 expresses experience; 去了 would just report that he went.

exercises.q: 过 is negated with 没: 我没去过日本。
exercises.explain: Experience is negated with 没...过, and 过 stays.

exercises.answer: 我 没 吃 早饭。
他 在 看 书 呢。

exercises.q: 'She is eating right now.'
exercises.explain: 正在 before the verb marks an action in progress.

exercises.q: 门开___。(the door is open – continuing state)
exercises.explain: 着 after the verb describes the state that results.

exercises.q: 他笑___说。(said with a smile – manner)
exercises.explain: Verb + 着 + verb shows the manner of the second action.

exercises.q: 我每天吃了早饭。 is the correct way to say 'I eat breakfast every day'.
exercises.explain: Habitual actions take no 了: 我每天吃早饭.

exercises.answer: 我 学 了 两年 中文。
exercises.en: I studied Chinese for two years.

exercises.q: 我不去了。 means
exercises.explain: 不 + verb + final 了 marks a change of plan.

exercises.q: Which sentence means 'I've eaten (already)'?
exercises.explain: Final 了 after a bare object marks that the event has happened.

exercises.q: 着 is used after verbs like 坐, 站, 开, 穿 to describe a continuing state, as in 他穿着红衣服。
exercises.explain: The state of sitting, standing, being open or wearing is marked with 着.

exercises.q: 他们___吃饭呢。(in the middle of eating)
exercises.explain: 在 or 正在 before the verb marks an action in progress; 呢 reinforces it.

exercises.q: 快下雨了。
exercises.explain: 快...了 frames an imminent event.

exercises.answer: 你 吃 过 北京 烤鸭 吗？
exercises.en: Have you ever eaten Peking duck?

exercises.q: 'I have never been to Shanghai.'
exercises.explain: 从来没...过 means 'never' as experience.

exercises.q: In 我学了两年中文了, the second 了 shows that the studying continues up to now.
exercises.explain: Verb-了 + duration + final 了 means 'have been doing so far'.

exercises.q: Which is NOT a correct use of 了?
exercises.explain: 是 does not take verb-了; a change of state uses final 了: 他是老师了.

exercises.q: 墙上挂___一张画。(hanging – continuing state)
exercises.explain: Place + verb + 着 describes what is located somewhere.

exercises.q: 'He came.' (the event has happened)
exercises.explain: 来了 reports that the event has happened; 来过 would mean 'has been here before'.

exercises.q: Sentence-final 了 can mark a new situation: 他二十岁了 'he is twenty now'.
exercises.explain: Final 了 after an age or state means it has now been reached.

pairs: negates habits, intentions and the future

sections.title: Adjectives, 很, comparison with 比 and degree
sections.summary: Chinese adjectives work as verbs: they stand alone as the predicate and take adverbs of degree such as 很, 太...了 and 一点儿. This chapter also covers comparison with 比, 没有 and 一样, and the superlative 最.

rules.title: Adjectives are predicates without 是
rules.body: An adjective can be the whole predicate; no 是 is needed: 我忙 'I am busy', 这个贵 'this is expensive'. In a plain statement a bare adjective sounds like a contrast (我忙，他不忙 'I'm busy, he isn't'), so the adverb 很 hěn is added as a filler with little or no meaning of 'very': 我很忙 'I'm busy', 她很漂亮 'she is pretty'.

examples.en: I'm busy, he isn't. (contrast, no 很)

rules.title: Negation and questions with adjectives
rules.body: Negate with 不: 不忙 'not busy', 不贵 'not expensive', 不太贵 'not too expensive'. Yes/no questions use 吗 or A-not-A, without 很: 你忙吗？ / 你忙不忙？ 'Are you busy?'. Answer with the adjective: 忙 / 不忙.

rules.title: Adverbs of degree: 很, 非常, 真, 比较
rules.body: Adverbs go before the adjective. 很 hěn very (often weak), 非常 fēicháng extremely, 真 zhēn really, 比较 bǐjiào fairly, 特别 tèbié especially. Stress 很 in speech to make it mean 'very'. 不太 bú tài means 'not very': 不太好 'not so good'.

rules.title: 太...了: too, extremely
rules.body: 太 tài before the adjective with 了 at the end means 'too' or, as an exclamation, 'so': 太贵了 'too expensive!', 太好了 'great!', 太热了 'it's so hot'. The negative 不太 drops the 了: 不太贵. 了 here is the sentence-final particle of the previous chapter, marking an evaluation.

rules.title: 有点儿 before, 一点儿 after
rules.body: 有点儿 yǒudiǎnr 'a bit' goes before the adjective and usually expresses something unwelcome: 有点儿贵 'a bit expensive', 有点儿累 'a bit tired'. 一点儿 yìdiǎnr goes after the adjective and means 'a little more', as in comparisons and requests: 便宜一点儿 'a bit cheaper', 快一点儿 'a bit faster'. 一点儿 never precedes an adjective.

examples.en: Please speak a bit more slowly.

rules.title: Comparison with 比
rules.body: A 比 B + adjective means 'A is more ... than B': 我比他高 'I am taller than him', 今天比昨天冷 'today is colder than yesterday'. Do not add 很 or 非常 after 比; to intensify use 更 gèng or 还 hái before the adjective (我比他更高), or put the degree after it: 高一点儿 'a bit taller', 高得多 'much taller', 大三岁 'three years older'.

examples.roman: Tā bǐ wǒ dà sān suì.
examples.en: He is three years older than me.

examples.roman: Zhège bǐ nàge guì de duō.
examples.en: This is much more expensive than that.

rules.title: Not as ... as: 没有
rules.body: To say A is less than B, use A 没有 B (这么/那么) + adjective: 我没有他高 'I am not as tall as he is', 上海没有北京冷 'Shanghai is not as cold as Beijing'. A 不比 B + adjective means only 'A is not more ... than B' and often implies they are about the same, so 没有 is the usual negative.

examples.en: I am not as tall as him.
Shanghai is not as cold as Beijing.
He is not taller than me.

rules.title: Equality: 跟 ... 一样
rules.body: A 跟 B 一样 + adjective says the two are alike: 我跟他一样高 'I am as tall as he is', 这个跟那个一样贵 'this is as expensive as that'. 和 hé can replace 跟 gēn. Without an adjective, 一样 means 'the same': 我们的书一样; the negative is 不一样.

examples.en: I am as tall as him.
This is as expensive as that.
Our books are not the same.

rules.title: Superlative with 最
rules.body: 最 zuì before an adjective gives the superlative: 最大 biggest, 最好 best, 最贵 most expensive. 最 + adjective + 的 modifies a noun: 最好的朋友 'best friend', 最大的城市 'the biggest city'. 最 also works with verbs of liking: 我最喜欢茶 'I like tea most'.

examples.roman: Zhè shì zuì hǎo de fànguǎn.

examples.en: I like tea most of all.

rules.title: Adjectives before nouns
rules.body: A one-syllable adjective modifies a noun directly: 好人 'good person', 大城市 'big city', 新书 'new book'. Two-syllable adjectives and any adjective with an adverb take 的: 漂亮的花 'beautiful flowers', 很大的房子 'a very big house', 最好的朋友. The modifier always comes before the noun.

exercises.q: 'I am busy.'
exercises.explain: Adjectives take 很, not 是, in a plain statement.

exercises.q: 她___漂亮。(the usual filler adverb, 'very')
exercises.explain: 很 fills the slot before a predicate adjective, with little force of 'very'.

exercises.q: Adjectives are usually joined to the subject with 是, as in English 'is'.
exercises.explain: Adjectives are predicates by themselves: 我很忙, not 我是忙.

exercises.q: 'Too expensive!'
exercises.explain: 太 + adjective + 了 means 'too ...'.

exercises.q: 'I am taller than him.'
exercises.explain: A 比 B + adjective; no 很 after 比.

exercises.q: 今天___昨天冷。(than)
exercises.explain: 比 stands between the two things compared.

exercises.q: You can say 我比他很高 to mean 'I am much taller than him'.
exercises.explain: 很 cannot follow 比; say 我比他高得多 or 我比他更高.

exercises.q: 'a bit cheaper'

exercises.q: 这个有点儿贵。 means
options: This is a bit expensive (and that's a problem).

exercises.answer: 我 比 他 高。
今天 太 热 了。

exercises.explain: 跟...一样 + adjective expresses equality.

exercises.q: 'the best'
exercises.explain: 最 + adjective is the superlative; 的 links it to a noun.

exercises.q: 最 goes before the adjective: 最大 'the biggest'.
exercises.explain: Degree words, including 最, always precede the adjective.

exercises.q: 'a beautiful city'
exercises.explain: Two-syllable adjectives take 的 before the noun.

exercises.q: One-syllable adjectives can modify a noun directly without 的: 好人, 大城市.
exercises.explain: Short adjectives attach directly; longer or modified ones need 的.

exercises.answer: 他 比 我 大 三 岁。
exercises.en: He is three years older than me.

exercises.q: 'much more expensive'
exercises.explain: Adjective + 得多 expresses a big difference.

exercises.q: 这个菜___好吃了！(so delicious)
exercises.explain: 太...了 is the exclamation 'so / too ...!'

exercises.q: 我忙，他不忙。 Without 很, the bare adjective suggests
exercises.explain: A bare adjective predicate invites a comparison or contrast.

pairs: I am not as tall as him.
I am as tall as him.

exercises.q: 一点儿 goes before the adjective: 一点儿贵.
exercises.explain: 一点儿 follows the adjective (贵一点儿); it is 有点儿 that goes before.

exercises.q: Negate 她很高。 ('She is not tall.')
exercises.explain: Adjectives are negated with 不.

exercises.answer: 这 是 最 好 的 饭馆。

exercises.q: 'even taller': 他比我___高。
exercises.explain: 更 (or 还) intensifies a 比 comparison.

exercises.q: 我___他一样大。(with / and, in an equal comparison)
exercises.explain: 跟 or 和 links the two items before 一样.

exercises.q: 非常 means 'extremely' and goes before the adjective: 非常好.
exercises.explain: Degree adverbs precede the adjective.

sections.title: The particle 的, possession and modification
sections.summary: 的 is the most frequent character in Chinese. It links a possessor, an adjective or a whole clause to the noun that follows, stands alone as 'the ... one', and forms the 是...的 pattern for emphasis. This chapter also distinguishes 的 from its siblings 地 and 得.

rules.title: Possession: X 的 Y
rules.body: Put 的 de between the owner and the thing owned: 我的书 'my book', 他的车 'his car', 老师的名字 'the teacher's name', 中国的历史 'China's history'. There are no separate possessive pronouns; 我的, 你的, 他的 cover my, your, his.

rules.title: Dropping 的 with family, friends and groups
rules.body: After a pronoun, 的 is usually left out before family members, close people and the groups you belong to: 我妈妈 'my mum', 我朋友 'my friend', 我家 'my home', 我们学校 'our school', 他们公司 'their company'. Keeping 的 (我的妈妈) is not wrong, just slightly formal or emphatic.

rules.title: Adjective + 的 + noun
rules.body: Two-syllable adjectives and any adjective with an adverb link to the noun with 的: 漂亮的花 'beautiful flowers', 很大的房子 'a very big house', 最好的朋友 'best friend'. One-syllable adjectives usually attach directly: 好人, 新书, 大城市, though 的 appears for emphasis.

rules.title: Clauses before the noun: 'the book I bought'
rules.body: Chinese has no words like 'who' or 'which' for relative clauses. The describing clause goes before the noun and is joined by 的: 我买的书 'the book I bought', 说中文的人 'people who speak Chinese', 穿红衣服的女孩 'the girl wearing red', 昨天来的朋友 'the friend who came yesterday'. The noun always comes last.

examples.roman: Wǒ mǎi de shū hěn guì.
examples.en: The book I bought is expensive.

examples.roman: Shuō Zhōngwén de rén hěn duō.
examples.en: There are many people who speak Chinese.

examples.target: 穿红衣服的女孩是我妹妹。
examples.roman: Chuān hóng yīfu de nǚhái shì wǒ mèimei.
examples.en: The girl in red is my younger sister.

rules.title: 的 standing alone: 'the ... one'
rules.body: When the noun is clear from context, drop it and let 的 carry the phrase: 这是我的 'this is mine', 我要红的 'I want the red one', 大的太贵了 'the big one is too expensive', 这是我买的 'this is the one I bought'.

examples.en: The big one is too expensive.

rules.title: Noun + noun without 的
rules.body: When the first noun names a kind or category rather than an owner, no 的 is used: 中文书 'a Chinese-language book', 中国人 'a Chinese person', 英语老师 'an English teacher', 北京大学 'Peking University', 木头桌子 'a wooden table'. Compare 老师的书 'the teacher's book' with 中文书 'a Chinese book'.

rules.title: 是...的 for emphasis
rules.body: To stress when, where, how or with whom a past event happened, put 是 before that detail and 的 at the end: 我是昨天来的 'it was yesterday that I came', 他是坐飞机来的 'he came by plane', 我是在北京学的中文 'I learned Chinese in Beijing'. The question form asks for the detail: 你是什么时候来的？ 'When did you come?'. 是 can be dropped in speech, 的 cannot.

examples.roman: Tā shì zuò fēijī lái de.
Nǐ shì shénme shíhou lái de?

rules.title: The three de: 的, 地, 得
rules.body: All three are pronounced de but have different jobs. 的 links a modifier to a noun (我的书, 漂亮的花). 地 links an adverb to a verb that follows: 慢慢地走 'walk slowly', 高兴地说 'say happily'. 得 follows a verb and introduces a complement describing how well or to what degree: 说得很好 'speak very well', 跑得很快 'run fast'. Rule of thumb: 的 before nouns, 地 before verbs, 得 after verbs.

examples.en: He speaks very well. (得 after the verb)

rules.title: Stacking modifiers
rules.body: When several modifiers describe one noun, the usual order is possessor, then demonstrative + number + measure word, then adjective, then the noun: 我的那本新书 'that new book of mine', 他的两个好朋友 'his two good friends'. With a pronoun possessor the 的 is often dropped: 我那本书.

examples.roman: wǒ de nà běn xīn shū
tā de liǎng ge hǎo péngyou

examples.en: Where is that book of mine?

exercises.q: 'my book'
exercises.explain: Possessor + 的 + noun.

exercises.q: 这是老师___车。(possessive)
exercises.explain: 的 links the owner 老师 to 车.

exercises.q: With close family members, 的 is often dropped: 我妈妈.
exercises.explain: Pronoun + family word usually needs no 的.

exercises.q: 'a very big house'
exercises.explain: An adjective with an adverb needs 的 before the noun.

exercises.q: 'the book I bought'
exercises.explain: The clause 我买 goes before the noun, linked by 的.

exercises.answer: 这 是 我 的 书。
我 买 的 书 很 贵。
exercises.en: The book I bought is expensive.

exercises.q: 说中文___人很多。(the people who speak Chinese)
exercises.explain: A describing clause is joined to its noun with 的.

exercises.q: In Chinese the relative clause comes after the noun, as in English 'the man who ...'.
exercises.explain: All modifiers, including clauses, come before the noun: 说中文的人.

exercises.q: 这是谁的？ means
exercises.explain: 谁的 is 'whose', with 的 standing for the thing.

exercises.q: Which phrase does NOT normally take 的?
exercises.explain: 中国人 names a category, so there is no 的.

exercises.q: 中文书 'Chinese-language book' takes no 的 because 中文 names a kind, not an owner.
exercises.explain: Category nouns attach directly; possession uses 的.

exercises.q: 我是昨天来___。(emphasizing when a past action happened)
exercises.explain: 是...的 brackets the detail being stressed.

exercises.q: 他是坐飞机来的。 emphasizes
exercises.explain: 是 sits before 坐飞机, the detail being stressed.

exercises.answer: 他 是 坐 飞机 来 的。

exercises.q: Choose the right de: 他说___很好。(he speaks well)
exercises.explain: 得 after a verb introduces a complement of degree.

exercises.q: Choose the right de: 他慢慢___走。(he walks slowly)
exercises.explain: 地 links an adverb to the verb that follows.

links an adverb to a verb
links a verb to a complement

exercises.explain: They sound alike; only the writing shows which is meant.

exercises.q: 'my older brother' (everyday form)
exercises.explain: Pronoun + family member usually drops 的.

exercises.q: 那个穿红衣服___女孩是我妹妹。(the girl wearing red)
exercises.explain: The clause 穿红衣服 modifies 女孩 through 的.

exercises.answer: 我 喜欢 红 的。

exercises.q: 'This is not mine.'
exercises.explain: 不是 + 我的, with 的 standing for the thing.

exercises.q: Modifiers (possessors, adjectives, clauses) always come before the noun they describe.
exercises.explain: The head noun is always last in a Chinese noun phrase.

exercises.q: 'the person who is speaking'
exercises.explain: Clause + 的 + noun: 说话的人.

exercises.q: 我妈妈___朋友是医生。(possessive)
exercises.explain: 妈妈的朋友: 的 marks possession between two nouns.

exercises.q: 'that new book of mine'
exercises.explain: Possessor, then demonstrative + measure word, then adjective, then noun.

exercises.q: 你是什么时候来的？ asks when someone came, using the 是...的 pattern.
exercises.explain: 是 before 什么时候 and final 的 focus the question on the time.

sections.title: Time, place and word order
sections.summary: Chinese word order is strict about where time and place go: both come before the verb, time first. This chapter covers time words, telling the time, durations after the verb, 在, 从...到..., distance with 离 and expressions of frequency.

rules.title: Time goes before the verb
rules.body: A time expression stands before the verb, either after the subject or at the very start of the sentence: 我明天去北京 or 明天我去北京 'I'm going to Beijing tomorrow'. Unlike English, it cannot go at the end: 我去北京明天 is wrong. Time words include 今天 today, 明天 tomorrow, 昨天 yesterday, 现在 now, 每天 every day, 晚上 evening.

examples.en: He watches TV in the evening.

rules.title: From big to small
rules.body: Dates and times go from the largest unit to the smallest: year, month, day, weekday, part of day, hour, minute: 2026年10月19日星期一上午九点 'Monday 19 October 2026, 9 a.m.'. Years are read digit by digit: 2026年 èr líng èr liù nián. Months are numbered: 一月 January, 十二月 December; weekdays are 星期一 Monday to 星期六 Saturday and 星期天 / 星期日 Sunday.

examples.roman: èr líng èr liù nián shí yuè shí jiǔ rì

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.body: Hours use 点 diǎn and minutes 分 fēn: 三点十分 3:10, 八点半 8:30 (半 half), 三点一刻 3:15 (刻 quarter), 差五分九点 8:55 (差 'short of'). 两点 is 2 o'clock (两, not 二). Add the part of the day before the hour: 上午九点 9 a.m., 下午三点 3 p.m., 晚上八点 8 p.m.

rules.title: Point of time before the verb, duration after
rules.body: A time point (when) goes before the verb; a duration (how long) goes after it: 我八点上课 'I have class at eight' but 我上了两个小时课 'I had two hours of class'. With an object, the duration sits between verb and object (学了两年中文) or the verb is repeated (学中文学了两年). 我等了十分钟 'I waited ten minutes'.

examples.roman: Wǒ xué le liǎng nián Zhōngwén.
examples.en: I studied Chinese for two years.

rules.title: Place with 在, destination after 去
rules.body: Where an action happens is marked with 在 before the verb: 我在家工作 'I work at home'. A destination follows a motion verb directly: 我去北京 'I go to Beijing', 他回家 'he goes home', 我们到了上海 'we arrived in Shanghai'. Position words follow the noun: 桌子上 'on the table', 家里 'at home', 学校旁边 'next to the school'.

examples.en: The book is on the table.

rules.title: Time before place
rules.body: When a sentence has both a time and a place, the time comes first: subject + time + 在 place + verb + object. 我明天在家吃饭 'tomorrow I'll eat at home', 他每天在图书馆学习 'he studies in the library every day'. Other prepositional phrases such as 跟 'with' and 给 'to, for' also go in this slot before the verb: 我昨天跟朋友看电影, 我给他打电话.

examples.roman: Wǒ míngtiān zài jiā chī fàn.
Tā měi tiān zài túshūguǎn xuéxí.
examples.en: He studies in the library every day.

examples.roman: Wǒ zuótiān gēn péngyou kàn diànyǐng.
examples.en: I saw a film with friends yesterday.

rules.title: 从...到...: from ... to ...
rules.body: 从 cóng 'from' and 到 dào 'to' work for both places and times: 从北京到上海 'from Beijing to Shanghai', 从八点到五点 'from eight to five', 从星期一到星期五 'from Monday to Friday'. The whole phrase goes before the verb: 我从八点到五点工作. 离 lí expresses distance between two points: 我家离学校很近 'my home is close to the school'.

examples.roman: Cóng Běijīng dào Shànghǎi hěn yuǎn.
examples.en: From Beijing to Shanghai is far.

examples.roman: Wǒ cóng bā diǎn dào wǔ diǎn gōngzuò.
examples.en: I work from eight to five.

examples.roman: Wǒ jiā lí xuéxiào hěn jìn.
examples.en: My home is close to the school.

rules.title: Frequency
rules.body: Adverbs of frequency go before the verb: 每天 every day, 常常 often, 总是 always, 有时候 sometimes, 从来不 never: 我每天跑步, 他常常迟到, 我从来不喝咖啡. 'N times per period' is expressed with the period before the verb and the count after it: 我一个星期去两次 'I go twice a week', 一天三次 'three times a day'.

examples.roman: Wǒ yí ge xīngqī qù liǎng cì.

rules.title: Before, after and when: 以前, 以后, 的时候
rules.body: These words come at the end of the time clause, the opposite of English: 吃饭以前 'before eating', 下课以后 'after class', 我小的时候 'when I was little'. The time clause goes first: 下课以后，我们去吃饭 'after class we'll go and eat'. 上个星期 / 下个星期 mean last / next week, 去年 / 明年 last / next year.

examples.roman: Chī fàn yǐqián yào xǐ shǒu.
Xià kè yǐhòu, wǒmen qù chī fàn.
examples.en: After class we'll go and eat.

examples.roman: Wǒ xiǎo de shíhou zhù zài Běijīng.
examples.en: When I was little I lived in Beijing.

exercises.q: 'I'm going to Beijing tomorrow.'
exercises.explain: Time words go before the verb, not at the end.

exercises.q: 我每天___点起床。(at seven)
exercises.explain: 七点 'seven o'clock' goes before the verb 起床.

exercises.q: Time expressions usually go at the end of the sentence, as in English.
exercises.explain: They go before the verb: 我明天去, never 我去明天.

exercises.q: Write 'Monday, 19 October 2026' in Chinese order.
exercises.explain: Chinese goes from the largest unit to the smallest: year, month, day, weekday.

exercises.answer: 我 明天 在 家 吃饭。

exercises.q: 'I studied Chinese for two years.'
exercises.explain: A duration follows the verb and comes before the object.

exercises.q: A time point (明天, 八点) goes before the verb, but a duration (两年, 十分钟) goes after it.
exercises.explain: When = before the verb; how long = after the verb.

exercises.q: ___北京到上海 (from Beijing to Shanghai)
exercises.explain: 从...到... means 'from ... to ...'.

exercises.q: 'I run every day.'
exercises.explain: 每天 goes between subject and verb.

exercises.answer: 我 一个星期 去 两次。

exercises.q: 'half past eight'
exercises.explain: 半 'half' follows the hour: 八点半.

exercises.q: 现在三___十分。(o'clock)
exercises.explain: 点 marks the hour, 分 the minutes.

exercises.q: 星期天 and 星期日 both mean Sunday.
exercises.explain: Sunday has two names; the other days are numbered 一 to 六.

exercises.q: When a sentence has both, the order is subject + ___ + ___ + verb.
exercises.explain: Time comes before place: 我明天在家吃饭.

exercises.answer: 我 昨天 跟 朋友 去 看电影。
exercises.en: Yesterday I went to see a film with friends.

exercises.q: 'My home is close to the school.'
exercises.explain: A 离 B + 近/远: 离 and its object come before the adjective.

exercises.q: 下课___，我们去吃饭。(after)
exercises.explain: 以后 comes at the end of the time clause.

exercises.q: 以前 'before' and 以后 'after' come at the end of their time clause: 吃饭以前.
exercises.explain: The opposite of English: the clause comes first, then 以前 / 以后.

exercises.q: 'next week'
exercises.explain: 下 'down, next' gives next week; 上 gives last week.

exercises.answer: 我 小的时候 住在 北京。
exercises.en: When I was little I lived in Beijing.

exercises.q: 'I waited for ten minutes.'
exercises.explain: The duration goes after the verb: 等了十分钟.

exercises.q: 'I call him.' 我___打电话。
exercises.explain: The 给 phrase goes before the verb: 我给他打电话.

exercises.q: In 我去北京 the destination follows the motion verb 去 directly.
exercises.explain: Destinations follow 去, 来, 到 and 回; only the location of an action uses 在 before the verb.

exercises.q: 我每天___八点到五点工作。(from)
exercises.explain: 从八点到五点 'from eight to five' goes before the verb.

exercises.q: 'three times a day'
exercises.explain: The period comes first, then the count: 一天三次.

exercises.answer: 从 北京 到 上海 很 远。
exercises.en: From Beijing to Shanghai is far.

exercises.q: Frequency adverbs such as 常常 'often' and 总是 'always' go before the verb.
exercises.explain: All adverbs precede the verb in Chinese.

exercises.q: 2026年 is read
options: liǎng qiān líng èr shí liù nián
exercises.explain: Years are read digit by digit.

sections.title: Modals, requests and complements
sections.summary: This chapter covers the modal verbs 想, 要, 会, 能 and 可以, polite requests with 请 and 吧, and the complements that complete a verb: result complements like 完 and 到, potential complements with 得/不, and degree complements with 得.

rules.title: 想 and 要: wanting
rules.body: 想 xiǎng + verb is 'would like to, feel like': 我想去中国 'I'd like to go to China', 我想喝茶. 要 yào is stronger, 'want to, am going to': 我要走了 'I'm leaving', 我要一杯咖啡 'I want a coffee' (要 + noun). The negatives differ: 不想 'don't feel like', while 不要 + verb is a command, 'don't!': 不要说话 'don't talk'. 别 bié is another way to say 'don't'.

examples.en: I'd like to go to China.
I want a cup of coffee.

rules.title: 会, 能, 可以: three kinds of 'can'
rules.body: 会 huì is a learned skill: 我会说中文 'I can speak Chinese', 他会游泳 'he can swim'; it also means 'will probably': 明天会下雨. 能 néng is physical ability or circumstances: 我今天不能来 'I can't come today', 你能帮我吗？ 'can you help me?'. 可以 kěyǐ is permission: 我可以进来吗？ 'may I come in?'. Negatives are 不会, 不能, 不可以; a refusal of permission is usually 不能 or 不行.

rules.title: 应该, 得 and 必须: should and must
rules.body: 应该 yīnggāi 'should, ought to': 你应该休息 'you should rest'. 得 děi 'have to' is colloquial: 我得走了 'I have to go'; its negative is 不用 bú yòng 'no need', never 不得. 必须 bìxū 'must' is stronger and more formal: 你必须来. 不用 also answers offers politely: 不用谢 'no need to thank me'.

rules.title: Requests with 请 and 一下
rules.body: 请 qǐng 'please' goes before the verb: 请坐 'please sit', 请进 'please come in', 请问 'excuse me, may I ask'. Adding 一下 yíxià after the verb, or doubling the verb (看看, 试试), makes a request lighter and more casual: 请等一下 'please wait a moment', 我看一下 'let me take a look'. 麻烦你 máfan nǐ 'sorry to trouble you' opens a polite request.

examples.en: Excuse me, where is the toilet?

rules.title: 吧 for suggestions and guesses
rules.body: 吧 ba at the end of a sentence softens it into a suggestion or mild command: 我们走吧 'let's go', 你休息一下吧 'why don't you rest a bit', 好吧 'all right then'. After a statement it marks a guess you expect to be confirmed: 你是学生吧？ 'you're a student, I suppose?'.

examples.en: Why don't you rest a bit.

rules.title: Result complements: 完, 到, 见, 懂, 好, 错
rules.body: A second element after the verb states the result: 吃完 finish eating, 看完 finish reading, 找到 find (search and reach), 买到 manage to buy, 看见 / 听见 see / hear, 听懂 / 看懂 understand by hearing / reading, 做好 do properly, 写错 write wrongly. They usually take 了 for a completed result and are negated with 没: 我没找到 'I didn't find it', 我没听懂 'I didn't understand'.

examples.roman: Wǒ zhǎo dào wǒ de shǒujī le.
Zhège zì wǒ xiě cuò le.

rules.title: Potential complements with 得 and 不
rules.body: Insert 得 de or 不 bu between the verb and its result complement to say whether the result can be achieved: 听得懂 'can understand', 听不懂 'can't understand', 买得到 / 买不到 'can / can't get', 做得完 / 做不完 'can / can't finish'. The question is 听得懂吗？ or 听得懂听不懂？. Note the contrast with 没: 我没做完 'I didn't finish' versus 我做不完 'I can't finish'.

examples.roman: Zhème duō zuòyè, wǒ zuò bu wán.
examples.en: So much homework, I can't finish it.

examples.roman: Zhè běn shū mǎi de dào.

rules.title: Degree complements with 得
rules.body: Verb + 得 + adjective phrase describes how an action is done: 他说得很好 'he speaks very well', 她跑得很快 'she runs fast', 你来得太晚了 'you came too late'. If there is an object, repeat the verb or front the object: 他说中文说得很好 or 他中文说得很好. The negative goes inside the complement: 说得不好.

examples.roman: Tā Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.

rules.title: Directional complements with 来 and 去
rules.body: 来 lái 'come' and 去 qù 'go' after a verb of motion show direction relative to the speaker: 进来 come in, 进去 go in, 出去 go out, 回来 come back, 上去 go up, 下来 come down, 带来 bring, 带去 take along. A place goes between the verb and 来/去: 回家去 'go back home', 进教室来 'come into the classroom'.

exercises.q: 'I would like to go to China.'
exercises.explain: 想 + verb expresses a wish; it goes before the verb.

exercises.q: Which modal expresses a learned skill? 你___说中文吗？
exercises.explain: 会 is 'can' for skills learned through study or practice.

exercises.q: 我___去中国。(would like to)
exercises.explain: 想 is the mild 'would like to'.

exercises.q: 可以 is used mainly for permission: 我可以进来吗？
exercises.explain: 可以 asks or grants permission; 会 and 能 cover ability.

exercises.q: 'Please sit down.'
exercises.explain: 请 goes before the verb.

exercises.q: ___问，洗手间在哪儿？(excuse me, may I ask)
exercises.explain: 请问 opens a polite question to a stranger.

exercises.q: 我们走___。(let's go – suggestion)
exercises.explain: 吧 turns a statement into a suggestion.

exercises.answer: 我们 去 吃饭 吧。

exercises.q: 吧 at the end can also express a guess: 你是学生吧？ 'You're a student, I suppose?'
exercises.explain: 吧 after a statement asks for confirmation of a guess.

exercises.q: 'I have finished eating.'
exercises.explain: 完 after the verb is the result 'finished'.

exercises.q: 我找___了我的手机。(found – result complement)
exercises.explain: 找到 'search and reach' is 'to find'.

exercises.q: 'I didn't find it.'
exercises.explain: A result that did not happen is negated with 没.

exercises.q: 'I can't understand (what I hear).'
exercises.explain: 不 between verb and complement makes the potential negative; 没听懂 would mean 'didn't understand'.

exercises.q: 你听___懂吗？(can you understand? – potential)
exercises.explain: 得 between verb and complement means the result can be achieved.

exercises.answer: 这个 字 我 写错 了。

exercises.q: Potential complements are formed by inserting 得 or 不 between the verb and its result: 买得到 / 买不到.
exercises.explain: 得 = can achieve, 不 = cannot achieve the result.

exercises.q: 'He speaks very well.'
exercises.explain: Verb + 得 + adjective phrase describes the manner.

exercises.answer: 他 中文 说 得 很 好。

exercises.q: 'Don't go!' (prohibition)
exercises.explain: 不要 + verb (or 别 + verb) is 'don't'.

exercises.q: 不要 + verb can mean 'don't' as a command.
exercises.explain: 不要说话 'don't talk'; 别 works the same way.

exercises.q: 'It will probably rain tomorrow.' 明天___下雨。
exercises.explain: 会 also expresses likelihood about the future.

exercises.q: 你___帮我一下吗？(can you, polite request)
exercises.explain: 能 (or 可以) asks whether someone is able and willing to help.

exercises.q: 等一下 means
exercises.explain: 一下 after a verb means 'briefly, a moment'.

exercises.answer: 请 等 一下。

exercises.q: 'I have to go now.' 我___走了。
exercises.explain: 得 děi before a verb means 'have to'.

exercises.q: The negative of 得 děi 'have to' is 不得.
exercises.explain: The negative is 不用 'no need to'.

exercises.q: 'I can't finish it (there is too much).'
exercises.explain: 做不完 is the potential 'cannot finish'; 没做完 only says 'didn't finish'.

exercises.q: 我看___他了。(saw him – result complement)
exercises.explain: 看见 (or 看到) is 'to see' as an achieved result.
